newsitem.title: USA: U.S. hints at Hizbollah link in Paraguay threat.
newsitem.headline: U.S. hints at Hizbollah link in Paraguay threat.

text.p: Officials said on Tuesday the U.S. Embassy in Asuncion, Paraguay, was threatened by an international guerrilla group, which they hinted could be the Iranian-backed Hizbollah.

The embassy said it was suspending all public celebrations of the U.S. presidential election after receiving a "terrorist threat." A statement on the threat was also issued later by the State Department in Washington.

Asked if Hizbollah, which is best known in Lebanon but also reportedly has affiliates in other countries, was behind the threat, a U.S. official who asked not to be identified said: "I wouldn't steer you away from that."
Another official said: "I don't think we're talking about indigenous groups here. We're talking about groups that operate on a global basis."

The Moslem fundamentalist Hizbollah has been blamed for past attacks in neighbouring Argentina that destroyed the Israeli Embassy in Buenos Aires in 1992, killing 29 people, and a Jewish community centre there in 1994, killing 86.
The State Department announcement said the new threat was directed "against official U.S. facilities in Asuncion."

"While there is no reason to believe that non-official Americans are the target of this threat, private U.S. citizens should exercise caution in their daily routines and in visiting U.S. government facilities or attending U.S. government sponsored activities," it said.
"This is solid information. We're very concerned about this," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
State Department officials said there were about 40 U.S. officials and their families in Paraguay, as well as some 200 Peace Corps volunteers and about 2,000 private Americans, mainly businessmen.
Apart from the embassy, they said, U.S. government buildings in Asuncion include a library and a cultural centre where election-night festivities were to have been held.

U.S. experts on Latin America suggested guerrillas might choose Paraguay to make an attack because of the relative ease of fleeing the country, particularly in a remote area where the borders of Paraguay, Argentina and Brazil come together.
"For 100 bucks (dollars) you can cross any of the three borders in any direction," one said.
